facts.text: The Lunar Module landed at 20:17:40 UT on 20 July 1969 in Mare Tranquillitatis (the Sea of Tranquility) at 0.67416° N, 23.47314° E.
The descent stage served as a platform for launching the ascent stage and was left behind on the Moon.
The descent stage had a dry mass of 2,034 kg and initially carried 8,248 kg of propellant. It held the landing rocket and its fuel tanks.
Armstrong stepped onto the surface at 02:56:15 UT on 21 July; the moonwalk ended at 05:11:13 UT. The astronauts collected 21.55 kg of lunar rock and soil.
The astronauts deployed the EASEP experiments; its laser ranging retroreflector (LRRR) is one of the arrays still used for laser ranging.
The ascent stage lifted off at 17:54:01 UT on 21 July 1969 after 21 hours, 36 minutes on the lunar surface.

NASA is working with industry to develop human landing systems (next-generation landers). As of November 2026, NASA's Artemis page says the first crewed Moon landing of the program will take place in 2028.
LROC (2012): 'the American flags are still standing and casting shadows at all of the sites, except Apollo 11.'
LROC (2012): 'Astronaut Buzz Aldrin reported that the flag was blown over by the exhaust from the ascent engine.'
Apollo 15 landed at 22:16:29 UT on 30 July 1971 at 26.13239° N, 3.63330° E, at the foot of the Apennine mountains near Hadley Rille. Its Lunar Module carried a Lunar Roving Vehicle.
The LRV had a 3-part chassis hinged in the center so it could be folded up and hung in the Lunar Module's quad 1 bay.
Each tire was made of zinc-coated woven steel strands 0.083 cm in diameter; titanium chevrons covered 50% of the contact area for traction. Each wheel had its own 0.25 hp electric motor.
Power came from two 36-volt silver-zinc non-rechargeable batteries.
On Apollo 15 the LRV was driven a total of 27.8 km. On Apollo 16 the vehicle traversed 26.7 km.
On Apollo 17 the rover went 35.9 km; its greatest range from the Lunar Module was 7.6 km.
The Apollo 15 astronauts collected 77.31 kg of rock and soil samples.
The LRV's last Apollo 15 drive was on the third moonwalk, on 2 August 1971.
NASA's Artemis page: 'NASA will send astronauts on increasingly difficult missions to explore more of the Moon.'
The astronauts of Apollo 11, Apollo 14 and Apollo 15 left retroreflector arrays on the Moon: arrays of prisms that reflect light back toward its source.
Apollo 14 landed on 5 February 1971 near the crater Fra Mauro. Its laser retroreflector (LRRR) is at 3.64417° S, 17.47865° W.
The Apollo 12 ALSEP science station included a passive seismometer and five other instruments, powered by a nuclear generator (RTG) that produced about 70 watts.
The Apollo 11 and 14 arrays have 100 quartz glass prisms (corner cubes) each; the Apollo 15 array has 300. The arrays require no power.
As of July 2019: four telescopes at observatories in New Mexico, France, Italy and Germany fire lasers at the arrays and time how long a pulse takes to return.
Laser ranging measures the Earth-Moon distance to within a few millimeters, and shows the distance increases by 3.8 cm (1.5 inches) a year.
Analysis of lunar laser data shows that the Moon has a fluid core.
The ALSEP stations were shut down on 30 September 1977.
The laser ranging experiment 'continues to return fresh data to this day' (NASA JPL, 2019). The Apollo 11 array was set up in July 1969.

Since 2021 the Apache Point station in New Mexico has been part of NASA's Space Geodesy Network. It routinely ranges several times a month to the three retroreflector arrays put on the Moon by the Apollo astronauts. In 2024 NASA published its full dataset, April 2006 to January 2024.
Surveyor 3 launched on April 17, 1967 and soft-landed at 00:04:17 UT on April 20, 1967 in southeastern Oceanus Procellarum (Ocean of Storms) at 3° S, 23.41° W.
Surveyor 3 bounced off the lunar surface twice, the first time to a height of 10 meters and the second to about 3 meters, before settling.
Via commands from Earth, the probe dug four trenches and performed four bearing tests and thirteen impact tests on the soil.
The spacecraft transmitted 6,326 TV pictures of the surrounding area.
The last contact with the spacecraft was May 4, 1967, two days after the lunar night began.
Apollo 12 landed about 180 meters from Surveyor 3. On November 19, 1969 the astronauts walked over and recovered parts, including the soil scoop and camera system.
The Apollo 12 moonwalkers were Conrad and Bean; they made two Moon walks.
NASA's Artemis page: 'NASA will send astronauts on increasingly difficult missions to explore more of the Moon.'
After the camera came back, scientists reported a small colony of the common bacterium Streptococcus mitis on it.

A 2011 review led by former NASA planetary protection officer John Rummel concluded the team 'only detected their own contamination'; people studying the camera wore short-sleeve scrubs, and the claim 'never passed peer review'.
Mars Pathfinder launched on Dec. 4, 1996 and landed on July 4, 1997 in Ares Vallis, at 19.33° N, 33.55° W (= 326.45° E).
Pathfinder delivered 'the first-ever robotic rover, Sojourner, to the Martian surface'. The rover weighed 10.6 kg (23 pounds) and stood 30 cm (1 foot) tall.
Protected by airbags, the lander 'bounced like a giant beach ball about 15 times, as high as 50 feet (15 meters)'.
Late on the second Martian day (sol 2), Sojourner stood up and rolled down the lander's rear ramp. It had been stowed against one of the lander's petals.
The mission returned more than 16,500 images from the lander and 550 images from the rover, and more than 15 chemical analyses of rocks and soil.
Rounded pebbles and cobbles suggested conglomerates that formed in running water during a warmer past.
The final data transmission was on Sept. 27, 1997; communications were lost for unknown reasons.
Spirit and Opportunity landed on Mars in January 2004.
Perseverance landed in Jezero Crater on Feb. 18, 2021, carrying the Ingenuity helicopter.

location.label: Meridiani Planum
location.note: The pin and local time are for Opportunity's landing site. It drove 45 km and rests in Perseverance Valley, on the rim of Endeavour Crater; NASA has not published exact coordinates for that spot.

facts.text: Opportunity landed in the Meridiani Planum region of Mars on Jan. 24, 2004 (U.S. time; Jan. 25 in Universal Time), at 1.946° S, 354.473° E.
'Designed to last just 90 Martian days and travel 1,100 yards (1,000 meters)', the mission spanned 2004 to 2019.
The rover has six wheels. Solar arrays generate up to 140 W under full Sun; the energy is stored in two rechargeable batteries.
Opportunity discovered spherules nicknamed 'blueberries': iron-rich concretions that formed inside deposits soaked with groundwater. Some are up to about 5 millimeters across.
Opportunity found hematite, a mineral that forms in water, at its landing site. Spirit and Opportunity confirmed that water was long standing on the surface of Mars in ancient times.
Opportunity holds the off-Earth roving distance record: 28.06 miles (45.16 kilometers), over a 14-year lifespan.
A severe Mars-wide dust storm blanketed the rover's location in June 2018. Opportunity last communicated with Earth on June 10, 2018.
After more than a thousand commands to restore contact, engineers made their last attempt on Feb. 12, 2019. NASA announced the end of the mission on Feb. 13, 2019.
The rover's final resting spot is Perseverance Valley.
Perseverance landed in Jezero Crater on Feb. 18, 2021.
Spirit landed at Gusev Crater in January 2004 (14.572° S, 175.478° E) and journeyed 7.7 kilometers (4.8 miles).
On 23 April 2009, Spirit broke through a thin crust into a pocket of sand that severely limited its mobility.
The last transmission from Spirit occurred on 22 March 2010.
Snopes rating 'Mostly False': the rover 'didn't actually send the words'; its final transmission was 'a bare-bones data dump indicating it was low on power as a storm approached'.
The quote originated in a Twitter thread by KPCC science reporter Jacob Margolis, who said the final transmission 'basically' translated as 'my battery is low and it's getting dark'.

location.label: Jezero Crater
location.note: The pin shows the Perseverance landing site in Jezero Crater. Ingenuity rests at its final airfield, nicknamed 'Valinor Hills', in the same crater; NASA has not published exact coordinates for that spot.

facts.text: Ingenuity landed on Mars on Feb. 18, 2021 in Jezero Crater, attached to the belly of the Perseverance rover (landing site 18.44° N, 77.45° E).
Designed for no more than five test flights in 30 days, the helicopter eventually completed 72 flights across nearly three years.
Mars' atmosphere is about 1% the density of Earth's at the surface. Ingenuity has two 1.2-meter counter-rotating rotors that spin at roughly 2,400 rpm.
Mass: about 1.8 kilograms (4.0 pounds on Earth).
The first flight, on 19 April 2021, lasted 39.1 seconds, hovering at 3 meters altitude: the first powered, controlled flight on another planet.
Ingenuity carries a small swatch of muslin from the lower-left wing of the Wright Brothers' Flyer 1, attached to a cable on the underside of its solar panel.
Ingenuity completed 128.8 flying minutes, covering 17.0 kilometers (10.5 miles) and reaching altitudes as high as 24.0 meters (78.7 feet).

On Flight 72 (Jan. 18, 2024) Ingenuity reached 12 meters and hovered for 4.5 seconds; about 1 meter above the surface on the way down it lost contact with the rover. Smooth sand ripples were hard for its navigation system to track.
Images showed the shadow of a damaged rotor blade; the helicopter is no longer capable of flight. NASA announced the end of the mission on Jan. 25, 2024.
Dragonfly, a rotorcraft, will fly to various locations on Saturn's moon Titan. As of November 2026 NASA lists launch as no earlier than July 2028 and arrival in late 2034.
The Ingenuity team nicknamed the spot where the helicopter completed its final flight 'Valinor Hills'. Perseverance photographed it there on Feb. 4, 2024, from about 450 meters away.
InSight launched May 5, 2018 and landed Nov. 26, 2018 on the western side of a flat, smooth plain called Elysium Planitia, at about 4.5° N, 135.9° E. It studied the deep interior of Mars.
InSight's robotic arm was 1.8 meters long. It lifted a seismometer and heat flow probe from the deck and placed them on the surface.
As seismic waves pass through or reflect off material in Mars' crust, mantle and core, they change in ways that reveal the depth and composition of those layers.
The seismometer detected 1,319 marsquakes.
An estimated magnitude 5 quake on May 4, 2022 (sol 1,222) is the largest quake ever detected on another planet. The previous record was magnitude 4.2.
The heat probe ('the mole') was designed to dig 5 meters deep but reached only about 40 cm because the clumpy soil gave it no traction. Its data still helps future digging missions.
Dust gradually accumulated on the solar panels and reduced power. Engineers used the arm's scoop to drop dirt on the panels on windy days, which helped sweep dust off.
The last contact was on Dec. 15, 2022. After two consecutive failed attempts to reach the lander, NASA announced its retirement on Dec. 21, 2022.
Studies of InSight's marsquake data continue; one found that rocky material that impacted Mars lies scattered in giant lumps throughout the planet's mantle.
Launched March 2, 1972. Pioneer 10 was NASA's first mission to the outer planets and the first spacecraft to fly beyond Mars, through the main asteroid belt, and past Jupiter.
Originally designed for a 21-month mission to fly by Jupiter, Pioneer 10 lasted more than 30 years.
First spacecraft to use all-nuclear electrical power: two SNAP-19 radioisotope thermal generators (RTGs) delivering about 140 W at Jupiter. It carried 11 scientific instruments.
The spacecraft entered the asteroid belt on July 15, 1972, emerging in February 1973.
Closest approach to Jupiter was at 02:26 UT Dec. 4, 1973, at a range of 130,354 kilometers. It took about 500 pictures of Jupiter's atmosphere.
Pioneer 10 crossed the orbit of Neptune on June 13, 1983, becoming the first human-made object to go beyond Neptune.
On Jan. 23, 2003 it sent its last signal from 12.23 billion kilometers; the signal took 11 hours and 20 minutes to reach Earth. Its RTG power had decayed too far to power the radio transmitter.
A final attempt to contact Pioneer 10 on March 4, 2006, failed.
Pioneer 10 carries an aluminum plaque with diagrams of a man and a woman, identifying the spacecraft's time and place of origin.
The spacecraft is generally heading in the direction of the red star Aldebaran and is expected to pass by it in about two million years.
Launched on March 6, 2009, Kepler was NASA's first planet-hunting mission. Objective: search for exoplanets.
Kepler detected planets by observing transits: tiny dips in the brightness of a star that occur when a planet crosses in front of the star.
The original goal was to monitor about 100,000 stars for three and a half years. The telescope's mirror was 1.4 meters (4 feet, 7 inches) in diameter.
The spacecraft required three functioning reaction wheels to position the telescope; in May 2013 it lost the second of its four wheels.
Kepler left a legacy of more than 2,600 planet discoveries from outside our solar system.
The mission revealed that our galaxy contains more planets than stars.
The K2 mission was expected to manage 10 observing campaigns with the remaining fuel; it reached 19 and raised the count of surveyed stars to more than 500,000.
Kepler ran out of the fuel needed for further science operations and NASA retired the spacecraft on Oct. 30, 2018, within its current, safe orbit.
The final 'goodnight' commands were received on Nov. 15, 2018. The spacecraft is drifting in a safe orbit around the Sun.
NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS), launched in April 2018, builds on Kepler's foundation, searching some 200,000 of the brightest and nearest stars.
